name: Burning glass
note: Seneca describes how a globe of water can concentrate sunlight to ignite. Rome already possesses this effect; neither lens nor glass shaping needed, just geometry.

name: Water-filled globe as magnifier
note: Spherical water containers magnify. The phenomenon is ancient and refraction geometry tells you why.

name: Polished metal mirror
note: Bronze and silver polished to reflect. Rome makes excellent mirrors; the technology is established.

name: Sundial
note: Shadow cast by the gnomon measures hour angle. Rome has precise designs based on latitude.

name: Water clock (clepsydra)
note: Steady flow of water through orifice marks time independent of sky. Rome perfected this and added geared indicator dials.

name: Groma (surveying cross)
note: Four arms with plumb bobs hung from crosspiece establish right angles for land survey. Roman roads and centuriation owe their precision to this.

name: Dioptra (sighting tube)
note: Tube with sights at each end (no lens) measures angles to distant marks. Hero describes gear-driven versions.

name: Steelyard balance
note: Unequal arms with movable weight on calibrated beam weighs goods without counter-weights. Rome has this; precision limited to roughly 1 percent.

name: Geared mechanical transmission
note: Bronze and iron gears with involute or cycloidal flanks transmit rotary motion at calculated ratios. The Antikythera mechanism shows Rome's capability.

name: Plano-convex reading lens
note: A flat surface facing text, one curved. Magnification roughly equals curvature radius divided by focal length. The blower must hold perfect sphere while cooling.

name: Spectacles (eyeglasses)
note: Two lenses mounted in a frame to correct presbyopia or myopia. Suspicion arises because it appears to grant unnatural vision. Matching a pair requires testing many lenses.

name: Spherometer for curvature measurement
note: Three legs at radius R, central screw measures sag of curved surface. Radius of curvature is computed from sag formula. Template surfaces act as control standard for grinding.

name: Focal length measurement
note: Form image of distant sun or window on screen, measure distance from lens to sharp image. Elementary but requires careful measurement and shielding from wind vibration.

name: Achromatic doublet lens
note: Crown and flint glass in contact correct chromatic aberration by choosing radii such that focal length is nearly independent of wavelength. Geometry demands extraordinary precision.

name: Apochromatic lens (three-glass)
note: Three glass elements correct chromatic aberration to smaller wavelength band than doublet, reducing false color to negligible in visual light. Requires flint and two crown varieties.

name: Speculum metal for telescope mirror
note: Copper-tin alloy with trace arsenic becomes hard and reflective. Cooling rate and composition affect color and tarnish rate. British Museum alloys show trial-and-error over decades.

name: Reflecting telescope (Newtonian)
note: Curved mirror of polished speculum focuses light; flat secondary deflects beam to eyepiece at side. Avoids chromatic aberration but requires frequent re-polishing.

name: Silvered glass mirror for telescope
note: Silver or mercury amalgam coated to glass substrate. More reflive than speculum and lasts longer between recleaning, but coating is fragile. Glass must be flat to better than 1 micron.

name: Equatorial telescope mount
note: One axis tilted parallel to Earth's axis. Rotating that axis alone keeps object centered as Earth spins. Requires precise latitude calculation and mechanical balance.

name: Clock drive for telescope tracking
note: Escapement-driven gear train rotates telescope at sidereal rate (slightly slower than solar rate). Accuracy to seconds per night demands temperature stability.

name: Transit instrument (meridian telescope)
note: Telescope pivots only in east-west, fixed in north-south. When star crosses meridian, exact time and altitude determine latitude and star position. Requires mercury basin for latitude check.

name: Stellar parallax and arcsecond precision
note: Star shifts position by one arcsecond from opposite ends of Earth's orbit if within ~3 light-years. Measurement demands micrometer precision, patience, and stable telescope. First measured by Bessel in 1838.

name: Diffraction grating
note: Tens of thousands of parallel lines 1 micron apart. Diffraction by equal spacing separates spectrum by wavelength more uniformly than prism. Made by ruling engine only.

name: Ruling engine for grating production
note: Machine whose sole purpose is scratching tens of thousands of equally spaced lines. Demands the finest lead screw in existence, thermal stability to microns, diamond tool, and 2 years of debugging.

name: Spectroscopy: emission line method
note: Heated element emits spectrum of lines, each element distinct. Allows identification of what is burning. Requires catalog of known lines and careful temperature control.

name: Spectroscopy: absorption line method
note: White light through cool gas shows dark lines where gas absorbs. Same elements produce same line positions. The complement of emission; requires bright background source.

name: Fraunhofer lines catalog
note: Mapping dark lines in solar spectrum and naming them by letter (H, K, D, etc). Over 500 lines exist. Requires years of careful observation and comparison with terrestrial sources.

name: Flame and spark spectra for element assay
note: Spark or flame emitted through sample salt identifies element by line pattern. Replaces classical wet analysis for many ores and minerals. Fast but requires reference samples.

name: Spectroheliograph (solar spectrograph)
note: Spectroscope coupled to telescope with narrow slit selects one wavelength from solar disk, mapping Sun in single element lines (H-alpha shows chromosphere structure). Requires perfect collimation.

name: Photometry and light measurement
note: Compare brightness of standard candles by visual contrast or disk photometer. Requires calibrated sources and standard atmospheric conditions. Historically done by Rumford.

name: Newton's rings interference pattern
note: Lens resting on flat glass shows concentric rings where air gap equals integer wavelengths. Wavelength of light can be computed from ring spacing. Elegant proof that light has finite wavelength.

name: Michelson interferometer
note: Split beam into two perpendicular paths, recombine, count fringes. Moving mirror one wavelength shifts fringes by two. Can measure distances to 0.1 micron. Requires rigid frame and ambient vibration isolation.

name: Nicol prism for polarized light
note: Calcite (Iceland spar) crystal cut and cemented at Brewster angle passes one polarization. Extraordinary ray refracted 90 degrees, separated by cement into wasted beam. Alignment precise to 1 degree.

name: Polarimeter for optical rotation
note: Light polarized by first Nicol passes through sample solution. Analyzer (second Nicol) rotated until extinction. Rotation angle tells sugar concentration. Sweet plant validation of physics.

name: Refractometer (Abbe design)
note: Sample between two prisms; critical angle marks boundary between dark and light regions. Scales directly in refractive index. Determines salt concentration and purity of liquids.

name: Abbe condenser (microscope illuminator)
note: Lens system below stage converges light from source onto specimen at angle equal to objective's aperture. Numerical aperture must match objective. Huge effect on contrast and resolution.

name: Oil immersion microscope objective
note: Oil between coverslip and lens increases numerical aperture. Requires lens design change and oil choice for index match. Cleaning lens after use is non-trivial; oil hardens if heated.

name: Phase contrast microscopy
note: Condenser annulus and objective phase plate convert invisible phase shifts (from transparent cells) into visible amplitude changes. Reveals internal structure without stain. Requires precise centering.

name: Ultramicroscope (dark field)
note: Slit illuminator sends light at grazing angle past objective aperture. Particles too small to resolve by normal microscopy (Tyndall effect) scatter light into objective as bright specs. Reveals colloid and virus sizes.

name: Electron microscope
note: Filament heated to emission in vacuum, electrons accelerated through 10-100 kV, focused by magnetic coils acting as lenses. Wavelength 0.1 nm allows 1 nm resolution. Requires bakeable vacuum chamber and careful filament life.

name: Sextant for angle measurement
note: Arc of 60 degrees, mirror and telescope measure angle to horizon. Tangent screw with vernier scale reads to 1 arcminute. At sea, determines latitude directly from sun or star altitude.

name: Artificial horizon for navigation
note: Mercury pool creates perfectly level reflecting surface. Sextant reflection doubled. Allows altitude measurement by boat even in rough seas. Mercury maintenance and capsule risk.

name: Theodolite (transit and altitude)
note: Telescope on two perpendicular pivots with graduated circles. Vernier scale reads horizontal and vertical angles to arcminute. Foundation of triangulation and mapping.

name: Optical level (surveying)
note: Telescope with bubble level establishes horizontal. Staff markings read through telescope. Detects height difference to 1 mm at 100 meters. Pendulum-damped level improves stability.

name: Plane table surveying
note: Telescope mounted on wooden board over map. Sighting to features and drawing lines produces map directly. Faster than theodolite but less precise; good for topographic detail.

name: Aneroid barometer
note: Partial vacuum box with corrugated brass diaphragm. Spring restores motion calibrated to mercury barometer. No mercury; portable and linear. Hysteresis and dial friction require friction compensation.

name: Hygrometer (humidity measurement)
note: Human hair lengthens and shortens with humidity (0-0.25 mm over 0-100 percent). Mechanical linkage magnifies to pointer on dial. Requires calibration by salt solutions.

name: Anemometer (wind speed)
note: Three or four cups catch wind, spin axle. Pulses close switch or increment counter. Calibration against standard wind tunnel difficult; approximation from rotation rate works to 10 percent.

name: Pitot tube (fluid velocity)
note: Two tubes: one faces flow (stagnation pressure), one is tangent (static pressure). Difference measured by manometer. Velocity = sqrt(2*g*h). Requires smooth entry and minimal blockage.

name: Manometer (pressure measurement)
note: U-tube with mercury. Pressure difference raises one column, depresses other. Read in mm Hg directly. Linearity to better than 1 percent across range 0-2 atm.

name: Bourdon pressure gauge
note: Oval brass tube coiled as helix; pressure forces straightening, rotates needle via linkage. Nonlinear response requires empirical dial calibration. Robust and field-durable.

name: Pyrometer by rod contraction
note: Metal rod held at measurement site cools slowly, shrinkage measured mechanically. Each alloy has known contraction rate; calibration by known temperature control required.

name: Pyrometer by thermocouple
note: Two dissimilar metals joined; junction heated, voltage measured by galvanometer. Nonlinear but reproducible. Platinum-rhodium allows temperatures to 1600 C.

name: Pyrometer by color (optical)
note: Spectral lines of tungsten filament shifted in position compared to heated object. Brightness match at one wavelength determines temperature. Requires calibration filament and dark room.

name: Pyrometer by radiation (Stefan-Boltzmann)
note: Lens focuses radiation from hot object onto bolometer or photocell. Power proportional to T^4. Non-contact measurement but requires emissivity correction and accurate focus.

name: Calorimeter (heat capacity apparatus)
note: Insulated container of water. Add fuel or material, measure temperature rise. Specific heat calculated from mass and T change. Precision limited by insulation imperfection.

name: Bolometer (radiation detector)
note: Thin platinum strip heated by incoming radiation, resistance change measured by bridge. Extremely sensitive but requires temperature control and isolation from air currents.

name: Photocell (photoelectric detector)
note: Cesium or other photoemissive surface in vacuum emits electrons when light strikes. Current amplified by dynamo or triode. Single photon detectable in dark conditions.

name: Seismograph (earthquake measurement)
note: Heavy mass damped by springs or pendulum. Frame sits on ground. Relative motion drives pen against rotating drum. Natural period of 10-20 seconds maximizes sensitivity to distant earthquakes.

name: Gravimeter (gravity field measurement)
note: Period of pendulum depends on local g. Measure period to 1 millisecond over many swings; gravity variations of 1 part in 1e6 detectable. Spring-based instruments avoid suspension issues.

name: Magnetometer (magnetic field measurement)
note: Magnetic needle deflects in field, angle measured against scale. Compass declination survey maps Earth's field; horizontal and vertical components separated by orientation changes.

name: Electrometer (charge measurement)
note: Galvanometer with high input impedance measures small currents from charged object. Quadrant electrometer achieves 1e-9 ampere sensitivity by using torque rather than deflection.

name: Potentiometer (precision voltage measurement)
note: Known voltage (from standard cell) balanced against unknown via null galvanometer. Sliding contact on calibrated wire determines ratio. Zero-current measurement avoids galvanic heating.

name: Ballistic galvanometer (charge measurement)
note: Moving coil over-damped with long period. Charge dumps in short pulse; coil swings proportionally. Integral of current over time measured without recording. Detects magnetic flux changes.

name: Oscilloscope (CRT time-display)
note: Cathode ray tube, beam deflected by time-base and signal voltages. Traces waveform directly on screen. Requires 1000+ volt HT supply and precise synchronization.

name: Chronograph (time marker)
note: Vibrating tuning fork marks dots on paper tape at 100 Hz. Paper moves at known speed, displacement read in milliseconds. Measures bullet transit time and explosives detonation intervals.

name: Stroboscope (periodic light)
note: Rotating disk or electric lamp flash synchronized to object rotation freezes motion. Variable frequency allows measuring RPM directly. Spectator error (aliasing) common.

name: High speed camera
note: Multiple rotating drum with lenses or rotating mirror. Exposes film at 1000 frames per second. Shutter speed below 1 microsecond by mechanical or electrical gating. Film advance is challenge.

name: Standards laboratory as institution
note: Building, personnel, standards, and equipment to maintain national measures. Meter bar, kilogram weight, temperature scale, density standards. Traceability requires stability and isolation from vibration.
